$comment: VENDORED COPY. The backend owns the original of this file; re-vendor it from there rather than editing here. Everything below is that file's own comment, unchanged.
The vocabularies a paired client is allowed to put on the wire: event types,
sources, and tool types.
This file exists because each of these was hand-authored twice with no
mechanical link between the copies -- AscendaTelemetryEventType and
AscendaTelemetrySource in ai-engineer-tools' packages/tool-contract (TypeScript),
and WorkloadCategoryMap / KnownSources / KnownToolTypes in
Services/ToolTelemetryCatalog.cs (C#). Drift between them did not fail a build.
It surfaced as rows in the 'unclassified' bucket months later, which is how
@ascenda-one/history-import lost seven months of one person's history behind a
2xx; and as code_forge, which ascenda-github-collector has always sent and
KnownSources never listed, harmless only because IsKnownSource is not consulted
at ingest.
v1 covered eventTypes only, which is precisely why the source drift went
unnoticed when the event-type drift was caught. v2 pins all three.
Ownership: this file is the source of truth for the wire vocabularies. The C#
side pins it in ToolPairingCatalogValidationTests; the TypeScript side vendors a
copy and asserts equality against its unions in wireVocabularyContract.test.mjs,
so a name added on one side and not the other fails a build rather than a
dashboard.
This file is enrolled in Contracts/vendored-copies.lock.json, so editing it also
reddens the fanout check here until ai-engineer-tools re-vendors. It was not, for
its whole first life: the ledger covered active-time-quantities.v1.json alone,
and this file -- built to the same pattern, in the same directory -- was checked
by nothing outside this repo. That is the same shape as the drift described
above, one level up.
The fanout diffs vendored COPIES of this file. A consumer that restates one of
these lists as a hand-typed array in its own source is not a copy and no fanout
run can see it -- packages/ide-extension-core's KNOWN_SOURCES is exactly that,
and being a subset of AscendaTelemetrySource it type-checks while missing a
name. Only a test in that repo, pinning the array against this contract, closes
that half.
Each list is the CLIENT-EMITTABLE set. The C# registries are deliberately
supersets of it:
- eventTypes omits the coarse workflow/HRIS types (email_activity,
message_activity, calendar_block), which the org activity-signals door mints
internally via CoarseSignalTypeMap rather than accepting from a paired client.
supervision_interruption WAS in that omitted group and no longer is. It was
server-side-only because nothing emitted it: the catalog has carried it (as
supervision, with an interruptionKind metadata key) since before any collector
could produce one, and only the pilot seeder ever wrote one. Claude Code's
Notification hook and Codex's PermissionRequest hook are what produce it, and
both are being registered -- so it becomes client-emittable here FIRST, because
ingest refuses unknown types per item and a collector that leads the catalog
loses those events permanently rather than retrying them.
- sources omits 'other', which is not a value a client sends but what
NormalizeSource substitutes for a blank one.
Enforcement differs per list, and the difference is deliberate:
- eventTypes IS enforced at ingest; an off-catalog type is rejected per item
with reason unknown_event_type.
- toolTypes IS enforced at pairing; an unknown toolType is a 400.
- sources is NOT enforced at ingest today. IsKnownSource exists and is tested
but is not consulted, so an unrecognised source is accepted and stored as
sent. It does not affect workloadCategory. Before wiring enforcement, audit
live traffic the way the event-type change did -- and note that
ResolveConsentType currently falls back to the ide_telemetry lease for an
unrecognised source, which is a consent question, not a vocabulary one.
